finalPass.decision:
All nine candidates stand on their evidence. The advisory lock itself now exists and is wired, but the PR moved contention from silent in-process waiting to a thrown, retry-instructing 409/503, and three of the sites that can now throw sit AFTER a commit with no catch: the staff post-merge sweep (#0, blocker — a retry re-folds the same items onto an already-merged order, a money double-count on the very path the PR protects), the post-create auto-consolidation across driver/customer/buyer/standing-order paths (#1, major), plus the sibling forceConsolidateCustomer callers left unread. The two client surfaces were not taught the new signal: mobile's 15 s axios timeout makes the 20 s wait contract unreachable (#2, major) and the offline drain classifies the transient 409 as permanent failure (#3, major). buyer.controller.ts was changed on a money path outside every package and outside acceptance A2, so it must be run through the money lens before merge rather than reverted (#4, major). Four minors in db-locks.ts and the sweep (#5 destroying healthy connections on timeout, #6 nullish-key fail-open, #7 type-based swallow, #8 head-of-line pool exhaustion) are cheap hardening the fixer should batch. Required before merge: catch-and-log lock-contention errors around every post-commit sweep/consolidation, align waitMs below the mobile client timeout, retry 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS in queue-drain, widen A2 to buyer.controller.ts and confirm the lens; then two more reads (forceConsolidateCustomer callers; the web merge payload/retry semantics) to confirm no further post-commit throw path and to fix the severity of #0.
Second read: The second read settled both questions. There IS a fourth post-commit path: order-templates.service.ts createOrderFromTemplate commits the order and then calls the now-locked mergeAllPendingForCustomer with no catch, so the new 409/503 escapes after the row exists and a retry duplicates the standing order — the per-customer catch given to sweepAllPendingOrders must be applied there too (major). The dashboard submit path posts delta items with no Idempotency-Key, so the server's in-lock replay guard can never fire for it; that means any 409 that escapes after a committed fold double-counts on retry, and the candidate stays major until the fixer confirms the controller's :203/:221 and buyer's :661/:688 post-merge sweeps were wrapped like the service sweep was (only the latter was verified in evidence) — if they are, the client gap is pre-existing and not this change's defect. The merge-pending-orders.js backfill is a fifth unlocked writer that contradicts the new "every merge serializes on the customer lock" claim; minor, fix by taking the same lock in the script. No further gaps — the run ends here.

findings.summary: waitMs is 20 000 ms but the mobile HTTP client aborts at 15 000 ms, so the designed "wait then 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS" contract is unreachable on the primary operator surface — contention shows up as a client-side timeout on a request that then commits server-side.
findings.detail: Every lock site uses `waitMs: 20_000` (orders.controller.ts:139, orders.service.ts:820 and :1167, buyer.controller.ts:552). `apps/mobile/lib/api-client.ts:9` creates the one shared axios instance with `timeout: 15000`. Sequence: operator A holds the customer key; operator B's mobile POST /orders (mergeChoice "merge") blocks inside `pg_advisory_lock`; at t=15 s axios raises ECONNABORTED and B's UI reports a failure; at t=16 s the server acquires the lock and COMMITS B's fold. `apps/mobile/lib/api-client.ts:147-148` (`const isTimeout = error.code === "ECONNABORTED" ...; const queueAsOffline = !isTimeout || isOnline === false`) deliberately does NOT queue a timeout while online, so nothing reconciles it — the operator sees an error for a merge that landed. The 409 body the API now produces can therefore never be observed by the mobile client for a wait-mode timeout: 20 000 > 15 000 by construction. The spec's Deploy-day note ("the web/mobile merge flows already handle 409 — MERGE_CHOICE_REQUIRED uses the same status") is also wrong on its own terms: both clients branch on the response CODE, not the status (apps/web/app/(dashboard)/orders/_components/CreateOrderModal.tsx:971-980, apps/mobile/components/NewOrderScreen.tsx:1846-1851), and neither knows MERGE_IN_PROGRESS.
findings.fixHint: Pick waitMs strictly below the tightest client timeout (e.g. 10 000 ms) so contention always surfaces as the intended 409 rather than a client abort, or raise the mobile timeout for the merge mutation specifically. Then teach both clients the MERGE_IN_PROGRESS code (auto-retry once, or a "someone else is merging" prompt) instead of the generic toast.
findings.decision: waitMs 20 000 at every lock site versus the single shared mobile axios instance at timeout 15 000 is a constant-vs-constant mismatch: a contended mobile merge always surfaces as ECONNABORTED (deliberately not queued while online) at t=15 s and then commits server-side at t=16 s. The designed 409 contract is unreachable on the primary operator surface; waitMs must sit below the client timeout or the client timeout must rise.

findings.summary: The offline queue classifies every 4xx as permanently non-retriable, so the new transient 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS turns a queued merge into a failed action the operator is told to re-enter by hand.
findings.detail: `queue-drain.ts:139-140`: `const isNonRetriableClientError = status !== undefined && status >= 400 && status < 500; if (isNonRetriableClientError) { ... failedActions.push(record) }`, and `describeFailedDrain` (:193-196) tells the operator "Nothing is resent automatically — re-enter the affected work." The new 409 the API emits (orders.controller.ts:191-194, orders.service.ts:1150-1154, buyer.controller.ts:646-649) is by design a TRANSIENT contention signal whose message is literally "...retry." — the one 4xx in the system that must be retried. Scenario: a driver's queued POST /orders drains while an operator merge holds the customer key; the drain gets 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS; the entry lands in `failedActions` and is never re-attempted; the driver is told to re-key the cart. Re-keying produces a fresh Idempotency-Key (apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts resets only on success or explicit clear, and a re-entered cart is a new cart), so if the original had in fact partially landed the re-entry can duplicate it. No API-side test can see this — the whole classification lives in the mobile package.
findings.fixHint: Add a retriable-4xx allow-list to `drainQueue` keyed on the response body code (at minimum MERGE_IN_PROGRESS) so those entries stay queued with the retry counter bumped, or return 503/429 instead of 409 for lock contention so the existing 5xx branch already handles it.
findings.decision: queue-drain.ts:139-140 classifies every 4xx as permanently non-retriable and tells the operator to re-key the work, but the new 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS is by design transient and its message literally says retry. The PR introduced the one 4xx that must be retried without teaching the only retry machinery to retry it, so a driver's queued order can be dropped for what was a 20 s contention window.

findings.summary: A 55P03 lock timeout sets failed = true, so the finally block destroys a perfectly healthy pooled connection on every contended wait — burning pool slots exactly when the pool is the bottleneck.
findings.detail: db-locks.ts:135-141: the acquire catch does `failure = e; failed = true;` before the 55P03 branch throws LockTimeoutError; :169 then runs `client.release(failure instanceof Error ? failure : ...)`, and pg-pool treats a truthy release argument as "destroy this client". But a `lock_timeout` on `pg_advisory_lock` leaves the session completely healthy: no lock was taken, no transaction is open, and node-postgres can reuse the connection. Concrete scenario: 8 merges contend on one hot customer; 7 block for 20 s and time out; all 7 backends are torn down and must be re-established (TCP + TLS + auth) instead of being handed straight to the next waiter. The pool is only `max: 8` (:64) with a 5 s `connectionTimeoutMillis` (:65), so the very next wave of merges — for any customer — can hit the 5 s checkout timeout while those replacements are still connecting and get LockUnavailableError -> 503, which per finding on orders.controller.ts:221 lands on requests whose order has already committed. The test cannot catch a change here either way: db-locks.spec.ts case (c) asserts only `expect(client.release).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` and never inspects the argument, unlike cases (b)/(g)/(i) which do.
findings.fixHint: On the 55P03 branch, throw LockTimeoutError WITHOUT setting `failed`/`failure` so the finally takes the clean `client.release()` path; keep the destroy path for the SET failure, an fn throw, and an unlock failure. Add `expect(client.release).toHaveBeenCalledWith()` to db-locks.spec.ts case (c).
findings.decision: On 55P03 the catch sets failed=true before throwing LockTimeoutError, and :169 releases with an Error, which pg-pool treats as destroy. A lock_timeout outside a transaction leaves the session healthy, so every contended wait burns and rebuilds a pool slot precisely when the 8-slot pool is the bottleneck, feeding the 503 path in #8.

findings.summary: withAdvisoryLock never validates family/key and wait mode never verifies the lock was actually taken, so a nullish key silently runs the critical section with no mutual exclusion.
findings.detail: `withAdvisoryLock` (db-locks.ts:100-171) passes `args = [opts.family, opts.key]` straight into `pg_advisory_lock(hashtext($1), hashtext($2))`. node-postgres binds `undefined` as SQL NULL; `hashtext(NULL)` is NULL, and `pg_advisory_lock` is strict, so it returns NULL and takes NO lock. Wait mode sets `let acquired = true` unconditionally (:130) and only inspects `res.rows[0]?.ok` for `try` mode (:132), so the helper reports `{acquired: true}` and runs `fn` completely unserialized — a fail-OPEN on a money path, with no log line and no error. It is not reachable from today's three callers (orders.controller.ts:101 narrows `dto.customerId` to truthy; the service takes `customerId: string`; buyer.controller.ts uses guard-populated `ctx.customerId`), but the module is explicitly built for reuse — discovery.md says PR-3's cron leader lock consumes this same helper — and this codebase reaches for `!` assertions freely on the very same value three lines below the lock call (orders.controller.ts:142, :154). Nothing in T1 or T4 would notice: T1 mocks the pg client entirely, so NULL-argument semantics never execute.
findings.fixHint: Guard at the top of withAdvisoryLock: reject a non-string or empty `family`/`key` with LockUnavailableError (or a TypeError) before connecting, and state the fail-open reason in the doc comment so future families cannot inherit it.
findings.decision: node-postgres binds undefined as NULL, hashtext(NULL) is NULL, pg_advisory_lock is strict and takes no lock, and wait mode hard-codes acquired=true, so a nullish key runs fn with no mutual exclusion and no signal. Not reachable from today's three callers, but the helper is explicitly built for reuse (PR-3 cron leader lock); a one-line guard on empty family/key closes a fail-open on a money primitive.

findings.summary: sweepAllPendingOrders swallows every ConflictException/ServiceUnavailableException by exception type rather than by lock cause, and its return value cannot distinguish a customer skipped for contention from one with nothing to merge.
findings.detail: orders.service.ts:1486-1498 wraps `mergeAllPendingForCustomer(g.customerId)` in `catch (e) { if (e instanceof ConflictException || e instanceof ServiceUnavailableException) { logger.warn(...); continue; } throw e; }` and returns `{customers: groups.length, merged}`. Two consequences. (a) The filter is by TYPE, not by cause: any ConflictException raised from deep inside the merge body — the transaction at :860+, `recomputeLineCategoryTaxes`, or (for the sibling `forceConsolidateCustomer` shape) `invoicesService.reconcileOrderDraftInvoice` — is now silently absorbed by the hourly cron and the `POST /orders/sweep` endpoint (orders.controller.ts:419) as if it were lock contention. Before this change any such error aborted the sweep loudly. (b) `merged` is only incremented on a truthy winner, and `mergeAllPendingForCustomer` also returns null when there was nothing to merge, so the response `{customers: 2, merged: 1}` (the exact shape pinned by orders.merge-lock.spec.ts T3-d) is identical whether the second customer was skipped because of a 20 s lock timeout or because they had a single pending order. An operator who presses "Consolidate all" during contention is told it succeeded, with the only evidence in a server log line.
findings.fixHint: Narrow the catch to the lock cause (check the ConflictException body's `code === "MERGE_IN_PROGRESS"`, or catch LockTimeoutError/LockUnavailableError inside mergeAllPendingForCustomer's caller before they are mapped), and return a `skipped` count alongside `customers`/`merged` so the endpoint's caller can see contention.
findings.decision: The sweep's catch at :1486-1498 filters by exception type, so any ConflictException/ServiceUnavailableException from inside the merge body is now absorbed by the hourly cron and POST /orders/sweep as if it were contention, where before it aborted loudly; and the {customers, merged} return cannot show a skipped customer. Discriminating on the MERGE_IN_PROGRESS code (or catching the lock errors before they are mapped) fixes both.

findings.summary: Waiters pin a pool connection for the whole 20 s wait, so contention on ONE customer exhausts the 8-slot pool and denies merges to every OTHER customer with a 503.
findings.detail: db-locks.ts:60-73 builds the lock pool with `max: 8` and `connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000`, and every caller — holder AND waiter — occupies one slot for the full critical section or the full `waitMs: 20_000` wait, because the wait happens inside `client.query(pg_advisory_lock ...)` on an already-checked-out client (:132). Concrete scenario: one busy customer receives 8 near-simultaneous merges (two scanners plus a buyer submit plus the cron sweep plus retries). One runs; seven sit blocked in Postgres holding all remaining slots. A ninth request — a merge for a COMPLETELY UNRELATED customer, which has no contention at all — cannot check out a connection, waits 5 s, and gets LockUnavailableError -> 503 "Merge lock unavailable". Head-of-line blocking on one key therefore takes out the whole merge subsystem for that API process, and (per the finding on orders.controller.ts:221) that 503 can land on a request whose order row has already committed. The pool sizing note in the spec's Deploy day section reasons only about the total connection budget, not about waiters occupying slots.
findings.fixHint: Decouple waiting from the pool: shorten waitMs (see the mobile-timeout finding), or acquire with `mode: "try"` plus a bounded application-level retry so a blocked caller releases its connection between attempts, or size the pool for expected concurrent waiters rather than expected concurrent holders.
findings.decision: Holders and waiters both pin a slot for the full critical section or the full 20 s wait, so eight merges on one hot customer exhaust the pool and an unrelated customer's uncontended merge hits the 5 s checkout timeout and gets 503. Real head-of-line blocking per API process; partly a designed capacity limit, but with #5 it compounds into 503s on paths that (per #1) can land after commit.

findings.summary: A fourth post-commit merge caller exists outside the controller/buyer/sweep set the fix rounds looked at: createOrderFromTemplate commits the order at :395 and then calls mergeAllPendingForCustomer at :418 with no catch, so the new 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS / 503 escapes to the client after the order row already exists — and the manual endpoint that reaches it has no idempotency guard, so the retry the error message invites duplicates the standing order.
findings.detail:
Call-site read (the question the decider asked me to settle: is there a fourth path?). Callers of the two now-locked service methods are: orders.controller.ts:203 (staff post-merge sweep), orders.controller.ts:221 (non-staff create sweep), buyer.controller.ts:661 and :688 (buyer sweeps), orders.service.ts:1487 (sweepAllPendingOrders — this one DID get a per-customer catch, verified at orders.service.ts:1488-1497), orders.controller.ts:426 (forceConsolidate endpoint — a bare pass-through with nothing committed before it, so it is fine), and order-templates.service.ts:418. That last one is in no work package, no spec covers it (order-templates.service.spec.ts:48 stubs mergeAllPendingForCustomer to resolve null), and it is the shape the fix rounds were worried about.

Failure path, concrete: an OPERATOR or CUSTOMER hits POST /order-templates/:id/generate (order-templates.controller.ts:88-93, @Roles(OPERATOR, CUSTOMER)) -> generateOrderForUser -> generateOrder (:217) -> createOrderFromTemplate. Line 395 commits `prisma.forTenant().order.create({...lineItems: {create: lineItemsData}})` — a standalone write, no enclosing transaction. Line 418 then calls `this.ordersService.mergeAllPendingForCustomer(template.customerId)`, which now (orders.service.ts:818, :1150-1158) can throw ConflictException{code:'MERGE_IN_PROGRESS'} on a 20s lock_timeout or ServiceUnavailableException when the 8-connection lock pool cannot hand out a client within connectionTimeoutMillis 5_000 (db-locks.ts:69-73). Nothing between :418 and the HTTP layer catches either. So: order committed, request answered 409/503.

Why that is money, not cosmetics: the manual path has NO idempotency guard — only the cron has one (`existing` check at :286-295). generateOrder mints a fresh `orderNumber = ORD-${Date.now()}` every call. The 409 body's message is literally "Another merge for this customer is in progress — retry.", and in the web dashboard it reaches the user as a toast (app/providers.tsx:36-38 — MERGE_IN_PROGRESS is not in HANDLED_CODES). The user retries -> a SECOND identical template order is created -> the next successful merge (hourly @Cron at orders.service.ts:1520) folds both into one winner, and mergeBoxedContributions SUMS the winner line with the loser contributions, so the customer's standing order lands at 2x quantity and invoices at 2x.

The cron path (generateDailyOrders :297-307) does catch, but miscounts: the order was created, yet the catch logs "Failed to generate order for template ..." and the template counts in neither totalCreated nor totalSkipped.

NOTE FOR DEDUPE: orders.controller.ts:221 (`create()` commits, then mergeAllPendingForCustomer with no catch) is the same shape; if the standing #0/#1 candidates only cover :203 and the buyer sweeps, :221 needs the same treatment. buyer.controller.ts:615-621 already states this exact rule in prose ("a throw here would report a merge that DID land as a failure ... the same cart would be added a second time") and applies best-effort catching to applyBuyerMergeHeader — then calls the sweep three lines later at :661 with no catch.
findings.fixHint: Make every post-commit sweep best-effort: wrap order-templates.service.ts:418 (and orders.controller.ts:221 / :203, buyer.controller.ts:661 if not already in the #0/#1 fix) in try/catch that logs the lock error and continues with the already-created/merged order, exactly as buyer.controller.ts:622-638 does for applyBuyerMergeHeader. A merge sweep that could not take the lock is deferred work the hourly cron will finish, not a failed request.
findings.decision: The call-site read establishes a fourth post-commit caller the fix rounds never touched: createOrderFromTemplate commits the order row, then calls the now-locked mergeAllPendingForCustomer with no catch, so the change's new 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS / 503 escapes to the client after the order exists and the generate endpoint has no idempotency guard, so the retry the message invites creates a duplicate standing order. Its spec stubs the merge to resolve null, so nothing pins this; the same per-customer catch applied to sweepAllPendingOrders belongs here.

findings.summary: Severity evidence for the post-commit-throw candidate: the web staff-merge posts DELTA items with no Idempotency-Key, so the server's in-lock replay guard can never fire for the dashboard — a 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS raised after the fold committed is indistinguishable from one raised before it, and the retry the toast asks for folds the same delta a second time.
findings.detail:
This settles the decider's second question. Payload shape: submitOrder builds `itemsForSubmit` at :902-927 purely from the modal's own `lineItems` (the new cart), NOT from the existing order's lines, and posts them with `mergeChoice: 'merge'` (:943). Server side, orders.controller.ts:158 does `foldMergeItems(current.lineItems ?? [], dto.items ?? [])` and writes the result with `replaceAll: true` (:168) — i.e. the delta is ADDED to whatever is currently stored. Re-posting the same body after a committed fold therefore double-counts (10 + 3 -> 13, retry -> 16), which is precisely the lost-update arithmetic the T2 concurrency pin exercises.

The one server-side guard against that is the replay check inside the lock (orders.controller.ts:151-157, findOrderIdByIdempotencyKey + recordIdempotencyKey at :180-182), and it is keyed on the `Idempotency-Key` header (:89, :93). The web client never sends one: useCreateOrder (apps/web/lib/api/orders.ts:277) is `apiClient.post("/orders", dto)` with no config, and the axios request interceptor (apps/web/lib/api-client.ts:103-121) attaches only Authorization and X-Tenant-Slug. The only idempotency work in the web app is in ScanInvoiceModal (a different flow). Mobile, by contrast, DOES send one per cart session (apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts, apps/mobile/lib/api/orders.ts:206) — so mobile is protected from this and the dashboard is not.

Retry is not hypothetical, it is instructed: MERGE_IN_PROGRESS is absent from HANDLED_CODES in app/providers.tsx:22-35, so MutationCache.onError toasts `data.message` = "Another merge for this customer is in progress — retry." (providers.tsx:37-38). onError in this file (:967-987) handles only MERGE_CHOICE_REQUIRED and the regulated-license block and does not call onClose(), so the modal stays open with the cart intact; the operator clicks Create Order again, gets the merge prompt again (:1034-1038), picks Merge (:1997), and the same delta is folded onto the already-merged order.

When the 409 comes from the lock ACQUIRE (LockTimeoutError, db-locks.ts:139-146) nothing was written and the retry is correct. When it comes from the post-commit sweep (orders.controller.ts:203) the write DID land and the retry over-charges. Both produce byte-identical 409 bodies. So the fix cannot live only in a client-side idempotency key — the controller must stop turning a post-commit sweep failure into an error response — but the missing Idempotency-Key is what removes the last safety net for the dashboard and should be closed alongside it.
findings.fixHint: Fix the server side first (make the post-merge sweep best-effort so a merge that committed is never reported as a failure). Additionally, mint one Idempotency-Key per CreateOrderModal cart session (mirroring apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts) and pass it as the Idempotency-Key header from useCreateOrder, so any retry of a merge that already landed replays instead of re-folding.
findings.decision: The payload evidence is solid: the dashboard posts delta items re-folded onto the stored lines with replaceAll and never sends an Idempotency-Key, so any 409 that escapes after the fold committed double-counts on the retry the toast requests. Whether such a post-commit 409 can reach the dashboard hinges on the controller's :203/:221 post-merge sweeps and the buyer's :661/:688 sweeps having been wrapped like sweepAllPendingOrders was — the evidence only verified the service sweep's catch, not those four — so this stays real until a fixer confirms every post-commit sweep in the controllers is caught (and if it is, the candidate collapses to a pre-existing client gap, not a defect of this change).

findings.summary: A fifth merge writer bypasses the new lock entirely: this backfill script re-implements the customer merge with its own PrismaClient and takes no advisory lock, so the invariant railway.toml, CLAUDE.md and the code map now assert ("order merges are cross-replica safe", "never add a second lock") is false for it.
findings.detail:
The PR's whole claim is that every customer-level merge serializes on ('order-merge', customerId): apps/api/railway.toml:9-12 now says "Order merges are cross-replica safe: staff create(), buyer createOrder and mergeAllPendingForCustomer/forceConsolidateCustomer serialize on a customer-keyed Postgres advisory lock", and .claude/code-map/api.md:604-611 enumerates the same four entry points. apps/api/scripts/merge-pending-orders.js is a fifth writer of the same rows and it is not in that set: it builds its own `new Pool({connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL})` + PrismaClient (:22-23), groups customers with >1 mergeable PENDING order (:26-38), and under `--execute` (:19, :42-46) re-reads and folds each customer's orders itself — the header even says "Mirrors OrdersService.mergeAllPendingForCustomer" (:4).

Failure scenario: an operator runs `node apps/api/scripts/merge-pending-orders.js --execute` against production (the documented usage at :11-13) while the API's hourly sweep (@Cron("0 * * * *"), orders.service.ts:1520) or a live staff merge is folding the same customer. The script reads the same PENDING orders, the API's locked merge commits, and the script then writes its own absolute totals derived from the pre-merge snapshot — the exact lost update B199 describes, silently, with no error. The advisory lock cannot help because the script never asks for it. The residual risk is small (a manual, one-shot backfill) but it is exactly the risk the new railway.toml comment tells a future reader no longer exists.
findings.fixHint: Either have the script take the same lock per customer before its fold (require the compiled db-locks helper, or issue pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('order-merge'), hashtext(customerId)) on its own pg client for each customer), or, if it is truly dead, delete it — and in either case make railway.toml/CLAUDE.md/api.md name the complete set of merge writers so the invariant stays checkable.
findings.decision: apps/api/scripts/merge-pending-orders.js re-implements the customer fold with its own Pool/PrismaClient under --execute and takes no advisory lock, so the invariant railway.toml, CLAUDE.md and the code map now assert is false for that writer. It is an operator-run backfill, not a request path, so the practical race window is narrow; the cheap fix is to take the same ('order-merge', customerId) lock in the script or document it as an offline-only tool.

confirmedFindings.summary: The lock pool has no `error` listener, so a dropped idle connection emits an unhandled EventEmitter 'error' and crashes the API process.
confirmedFindings.detail: `new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, max: 8 })` attaches no `pool.on("error", …)`. In the installed pg-pool (`node_modules/pg-pool/index.js:51-64`), `makeIdleListener` ends with `pool.emit('error', err, client)`; `Pool extends EventEmitter`, so emitting 'error' with zero listeners throws the error synchronously — out of the client's socket error handler, i.e. as an uncaughtException. I confirmed `grep -rn "uncaughtException|unhandledRejection" apps/api/src` (non-spec) returns nothing, so nothing in the app catches it: the process dies and Railway restarts it (`restartPolicyType = "ON_FAILURE"`), dropping every in-flight request and Socket.io connection. Trigger: any idle lock connection the server closes — a Postgres restart/failover, a Railway network blip, an admin `pg_terminate_backend`, or a server-side idle timeout. This is a NEW exposure, not a pre-existing one: the Prisma pool is safe precisely because `@prisma/adapter-pg` attaches this listener itself (`node_modules/@prisma/adapter-pg/dist/index.js:812-817`, `client.on("error", onIdleClientError)`). A pool this module owns gets no such protection for free.
confirmedFindings.fixHint: Attach a listener when the pool is created — `pool.on("error", (err) => logger.error({ err }, "db-locks idle client error"))` — so pg-pool's already-completed `_remove(client)` is the whole outcome and the emit has a consumer. Do not `process.exit` in it; the client is already purged.

confirmedFindings.summary: No `connectionTimeoutMillis` on a pool whose clients are pinned for the full 20 s wait, so the 9th concurrent merge waits in `pool.connect()` forever instead of getting the designed 503.
confirmedFindings.detail: The pool is `max: 8` and each `withAdvisoryLock` call holds its client from `connect()` through `SET lock_timeout` (up to `waitMs`, default 20_000 ms) plus the whole of `fn` (the merge's re-read, fold, `updateOrderItems` transaction with its own 15 s timeout, and `recordIdempotencyKey`). No `connectionTimeoutMillis` is passed. In `node_modules/pg-pool/index.js:199-232`, when the pool is full and `connectionTimeoutMillis` is falsy the waiter is pushed onto `_pendingQueue` with NO timer (`if (!this.options.connectionTimeoutMillis) { this._pendingQueue.push(...); return result }`) — the timeout branch below it is the only thing that ever rejects a queued waiter. Failure scenario: 9+ merge requests in flight at once (a BullMQ redelivery burst, or several scanners confirming on one busy customer while other customers merge concurrently) — 8 sit in Postgres waiting up to 20 s each, and the 9th and beyond hang in `pool.connect()` with no bound at all. That request neither returns 409 `MERGE_IN_PROGRESS` nor the `LockUnavailableError` → 503 the design promises; it simply never settles until the HTTP client gives up, and the worst-case wait is unbounded rather than the 20 s the spec advertises. The planned PR-3 cron leader lock, which by design holds its lock for the length of a cron run, would permanently consume one of the 8 slots and make this cheaper to hit.
confirmedFindings.fixHint: Pass an explicit `connectionTimeoutMillis` (a few seconds — well under `waitMs`) so pool exhaustion surfaces as the already-handled `pool.connect()` rejection → `LockUnavailableError` → 503, and consider whether `max: 8` is the right budget once a long-held leader lock shares the pool.

confirmedFindings.summary: The new pg.Pool has no 'error' listener, so an idle lock connection dropped by Postgres raises an unhandled 'error' event and kills the whole API process.
confirmedFindings.detail: db-locks.ts:54 does `pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, max: 8 })` and never subscribes to the pool's 'error' event. In pg 8.23.0, node_modules/pg-pool/index.js:51-63 installs an idle listener that ends with `pool.emit('error', err, client)`; `Pool extends EventEmitter`, so with no 'error' subscriber Node throws the error as an uncaught exception. `grep -rn "uncaughtException|unhandledRejection" apps/api/src` returns nothing — there is no process-level handler, and Nest installs none. Failure scenario: a merge finishes, `client.release()` returns the connection to this pool, it sits idle (this pool only wakes on merges, so idle is its normal state); Railway restarts Postgres or its TCP proxy reaps the idle socket; pg emits 'error' on the pool; the API process exits. railway.toml sets `restartPolicyType = "ON_FAILURE"`, so this becomes a restart loop under a flapping DB — a full multi-tenant API outage originating in a lock helper. The house's other pg.Pool is explicitly protected against exactly this: @prisma/adapter-pg/dist/index.js:813-817 attaches `client.on("error", onIdleClientError)` to the Pool it creates. This one is not. Related capacity note: the code uses `max: 8` while spec.md's Deploy day section says "Pool of 4 extra connections per API process" — the connection budget claim is half the real number.
confirmedFindings.fixHint: Attach a pool-level error handler at creation, e.g. `pool.on("error", (err) => logger.error({ err }, "advisory-lock pool idle client error"))`, mirroring @prisma/adapter-pg's onIdleClientError. Also reconcile max:8 with the spec's stated 4.

confirmedFindings.summary: db-locks.ts emits no logs on any failure path, and a failed pg_advisory_unlock is swallowed entirely — a stuck lock produces 409s with nothing in the logs identifying the family, key, or cause.
confirmedFindings.detail: The module has no logger. Three failure paths produce no signal: (1) db-locks.ts:124-128 — the UNLOCK query's error is caught and assigned to `failure` (`failure = failure ?? e`) and then never surfaced; the only observable consequence is the connection being destroyed by `client.release(failure)` at :135, which looks identical to a normal error-path release. A lock left held server-side because the UNLOCK failed is precisely the event that makes every subsequent merge for that customer wait 20s and then 409 — and it produces zero log lines. (2) db-locks.ts:93-95 — `LockUnavailableError(e)` captures the pg cause on the instance, but the planned controller mapping (build-plan.md p2) discards it into `new ServiceUnavailableException("Merge lock unavailable")`, so the underlying pg error (auth failure, DATABASE_URL wrong, pool exhausted, connection refused) never reaches Sentry or stdout. (3) db-locks.ts:111 — `LockTimeoutError` maps to a 409, which SentryExceptionFilter does not capture (it filters to >=500), so lock contention is invisible: there is no counter, no wait-duration log, no warn. remainingFindings.summary: The post-merge sweep runs after the fold has already committed but can now throw the new retry-instructing 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS / 503, and the web client has no Idempotency-Key, so the retry it asks for re-folds the same absolute totals onto an already-merged order.
remainingFindings.detail: Path: staff merge, web dashboard. (1) `orders.controller.ts:137-188` takes the customer advisory lock, folds and commits `updateOrderItems(..., replaceAll: true)` at :159 — order line for prod-1 goes 10 -> 13. (2) The lock is released at :188. (3) `:201-204` then calls `this.ordersService.mergeAllPendingForCustomer(dto.customerId)` with NO try/catch. That method now (orders.service.ts:818, :1148-1160) re-acquires the SAME (family="order-merge", key=customerId) lock and maps `LockTimeoutError` -> `ConflictException {code:"MERGE_IN_PROGRESS", message:"...retry."}` and `LockUnavailableError` -> `ServiceUnavailableException`. (4) If another holder (a second operator, a buyer submit at buyer.controller.ts:551, or the hourly `sweepAllPendingOrders` cron) holds the key across that 20 s window, or the 8-slot lock pool is saturated (db-locks.ts:64-65, 5 s connectionTimeoutMillis), the sweep throws and the exception propagates out of `create()` as the HTTP response — for a merge whose money write ALREADY COMMITTED at step 1. (5) The web client sends no Idempotency-Key at all (grep -i "idempotency" over apps/web returns only ScanInvoiceModal.tsx:188/376/1287 — nothing on the order-create path), so the controller's replay guard at :151-156 cannot fire. (6) `apps/web/app/providers.tsx:22-38` does not list MERGE_IN_PROGRESS in HANDLED_CODES, so the operator gets a toast reading literally "Another merge for this customer is in progress — retry."; `CreateOrderModal.tsx:967-987` only special-cases MERGE_CHOICE_REQUIRED, so the modal stays open with the cart intact. (7) The operator clicks Create again: `findActiveOrder` now returns qty 13, `foldMergeItems` adds the incoming 3 again -> 16. The customer is over-billed by one full incoming cart. The same shape exists at `apps/api/src/buyer/buyer.controller.ts:661` (sweep after the buyer fold committed at :608) — and that file's own comment at :615-621 spells out this exact hazard for `applyBuyerMergeHeader` ("a throw here would report a merge that DID land as a failure... the fold above computes ABSOLUTE totals, so the same cart would be added a second time") and wraps it in try/catch, then leaves the very next call, the sweep, unguarded.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Either wrap the post-write sweep in a catch that logs-and-continues (the sweep is best-effort; the merge has already landed and the cron sweep will reconcile), or hold one lock section across fold+sweep by inlining the sweep's body. Do not let a post-commit lock failure become the request's response, and never emit a "retry" 409 for a request whose write already committed.
remainingFindings.decision: The evidence shows the post-merge sweep at orders.controller.ts:201-204 runs after the fold committed and after the lock is released, with no catch, and mergeAllPendingForCustomer now re-acquires the same customer key and maps contention to a 409 whose message tells the caller to retry. A retry of a non-idempotent read→fold→replaceAll staff merge re-folds the incoming items onto an already-merged order — a money double-count introduced by this PR, on the exact path it exists to protect.

remainingFindings.summary: Post-create auto-consolidation now throws 409/503 for lock contention after the order row has already been committed, so a successful create is reported to the client as a failure.
remainingFindings.detail: `orders.controller.ts:211-226`: `this.ordersService.create(...)` commits a new order, then `:221` calls `mergeAllPendingForCustomer(created.customerId, {...})` for every non-staff (driver / customer) caller with no try/catch. Since orders.service.ts:818 that call can now reject with ConflictException(409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS) or ServiceUnavailableException(503) purely because another merge holds the customer key. The order exists; the caller is told the request failed. Same shape at `apps/api/src/buyer/buyer.controller.ts:688` (buyer create -> sweep) and `apps/api/src/order-templates/order-templates.service.ts:418` (standing order created at :395, then swept at :418). For the cron the blast radius is bounded — `order-templates.service.ts:297-307` catches per template — but `generateOrderForUser` (:254-257) has no catch, so an operator pressing "Generate now" sees a 409 for a standing order that was in fact created. Concrete scenario: two drivers submit orders for the same customer within the lock window; driver A's create commits and its sweep wins the lock, driver B's create commits and its sweep waits, times out at 20 s, and B receives 409 "...retry." for an order that is already in the database. B retries -> a second order for the same cart (no Idempotency-Key is sent on the buyer path; the mobile cart key at apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts is per cart session, so a fresh re-entry mints a new one) -> the next sweep folds both -> doubled quantities.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Treat the post-create consolidation as best-effort: catch ConflictException/ServiceUnavailableException from the sweep at orders.controller.ts:221, buyer.controller.ts:688 and order-templates.service.ts:418, log, and return the created order. The customer's orders will be consolidated by the next sweep.
remainingFindings.decision: Same post-commit shape: create commits the order row, then :221 calls the now-throwing mergeAllPendingForCustomer without a catch, so lock contention is reported as a failed create to drivers/customers, buyer create (:688) and the 'Generate now' standing-order path. The order exists while the client is told it failed; the fix is the same catch-and-log envelope as #0.

remainingFindings.summary: waitMs is 20 000 ms but the mobile HTTP client aborts at 15 000 ms, so the designed "wait then 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS" contract is unreachable on the primary operator surface — contention shows up as a client-side timeout on a request that then commits server-side.
remainingFindings.detail: Every lock site uses `waitMs: 20_000` (orders.controller.ts:139, orders.service.ts:820 and :1167, buyer.controller.ts:552). `apps/mobile/lib/api-client.ts:9` creates the one shared axios instance with `timeout: 15000`. Sequence: operator A holds the customer key; operator B's mobile POST /orders (mergeChoice "merge") blocks inside `pg_advisory_lock`; at t=15 s axios raises ECONNABORTED and B's UI reports a failure; at t=16 s the server acquires the lock and COMMITS B's fold. `apps/mobile/lib/api-client.ts:147-148` (`const isTimeout = error.code === "ECONNABORTED" ...; const queueAsOffline = !isTimeout || isOnline === false`) deliberately does NOT queue a timeout while online, so nothing reconciles it — the operator sees an error for a merge that landed. The 409 body the API now produces can therefore never be observed by the mobile client for a wait-mode timeout: 20 000 > 15 000 by construction. The spec's Deploy-day note ("the web/mobile merge flows already handle 409 — MERGE_CHOICE_REQUIRED uses the same status") is also wrong on its own terms: both clients branch on the response CODE, not the status (apps/web/app/(dashboard)/orders/_components/CreateOrderModal.tsx:971-980, apps/mobile/components/NewOrderScreen.tsx:1846-1851), and neither knows MERGE_IN_PROGRESS.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Pick waitMs strictly below the tightest client timeout (e.g. 10 000 ms) so contention always surfaces as the intended 409 rather than a client abort, or raise the mobile timeout for the merge mutation specifically. Then teach both clients the MERGE_IN_PROGRESS code (auto-retry once, or a "someone else is merging" prompt) instead of the generic toast.
remainingFindings.decision: waitMs 20 000 at every lock site versus the single shared mobile axios instance at timeout 15 000 is a constant-vs-constant mismatch: a contended mobile merge always surfaces as ECONNABORTED (deliberately not queued while online) at t=15 s and then commits server-side at t=16 s. The designed 409 contract is unreachable on the primary operator surface; waitMs must sit below the client timeout or the client timeout must rise.

remainingFindings.summary: The offline queue classifies every 4xx as permanently non-retriable, so the new transient 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS turns a queued merge into a failed action the operator is told to re-enter by hand.
remainingFindings.detail: `queue-drain.ts:139-140`: `const isNonRetriableClientError = status !== undefined && status >= 400 && status < 500; if (isNonRetriableClientError) { ... failedActions.push(record) }`, and `describeFailedDrain` (:193-196) tells the operator "Nothing is resent automatically — re-enter the affected work." The new 409 the API emits (orders.controller.ts:191-194, orders.service.ts:1150-1154, buyer.controller.ts:646-649) is by design a TRANSIENT contention signal whose message is literally "...retry." — the one 4xx in the system that must be retried. Scenario: a driver's queued POST /orders drains while an operator merge holds the customer key; the drain gets 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS; the entry lands in `failedActions` and is never re-attempted; the driver is told to re-key the cart. Re-keying produces a fresh Idempotency-Key (apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts resets only on success or explicit clear, and a re-entered cart is a new cart), so if the original had in fact partially landed the re-entry can duplicate it. No API-side test can see this — the whole classification lives in the mobile package.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Add a retriable-4xx allow-list to `drainQueue` keyed on the response body code (at minimum MERGE_IN_PROGRESS) so those entries stay queued with the retry counter bumped, or return 503/429 instead of 409 for lock contention so the existing 5xx branch already handles it.
remainingFindings.decision: queue-drain.ts:139-140 classifies every 4xx as permanently non-retriable and tells the operator to re-key the work, but the new 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS is by design transient and its message literally says retry. The PR introduced the one 4xx that must be retried without teaching the only retry machinery to retry it, so a driver's queued order can be dropped for what was a 20 s contention window.

remainingFindings.summary: A 55P03 lock timeout sets failed = true, so the finally block destroys a perfectly healthy pooled connection on every contended wait — burning pool slots exactly when the pool is the bottleneck.
remainingFindings.detail: db-locks.ts:135-141: the acquire catch does `failure = e; failed = true;` before the 55P03 branch throws LockTimeoutError; :169 then runs `client.release(failure instanceof Error ? failure : ...)`, and pg-pool treats a truthy release argument as "destroy this client". But a `lock_timeout` on `pg_advisory_lock` leaves the session completely healthy: no lock was taken, no transaction is open, and node-postgres can reuse the connection. Concrete scenario: 8 merges contend on one hot customer; 7 block for 20 s and time out; all 7 backends are torn down and must be re-established (TCP + TLS + auth) instead of being handed straight to the next waiter. The pool is only `max: 8` (:64) with a 5 s `connectionTimeoutMillis` (:65), so the very next wave of merges — for any customer — can hit the 5 s checkout timeout while those replacements are still connecting and get LockUnavailableError -> 503, which per finding on orders.controller.ts:221 lands on requests whose order has already committed. The test cannot catch a change here either way: db-locks.spec.ts case (c) asserts only `expect(client.release).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` and never inspects the argument, unlike cases (b)/(g)/(i) which do.
remainingFindings.fixHint: On the 55P03 branch, throw LockTimeoutError WITHOUT setting `failed`/`failure` so the finally takes the clean `client.release()` path; keep the destroy path for the SET failure, an fn throw, and an unlock failure. Add `expect(client.release).toHaveBeenCalledWith()` to db-locks.spec.ts case (c).
remainingFindings.decision: On 55P03 the catch sets failed=true before throwing LockTimeoutError, and :169 releases with an Error, which pg-pool treats as destroy. A lock_timeout outside a transaction leaves the session healthy, so every contended wait burns and rebuilds a pool slot precisely when the 8-slot pool is the bottleneck, feeding the 503 path in #8.

remainingFindings.summary: withAdvisoryLock never validates family/key and wait mode never verifies the lock was actually taken, so a nullish key silently runs the critical section with no mutual exclusion.
remainingFindings.detail: `withAdvisoryLock` (db-locks.ts:100-171) passes `args = [opts.family, opts.key]` straight into `pg_advisory_lock(hashtext($1), hashtext($2))`. node-postgres binds `undefined` as SQL NULL; `hashtext(NULL)` is NULL, and `pg_advisory_lock` is strict, so it returns NULL and takes NO lock. Wait mode sets `let acquired = true` unconditionally (:130) and only inspects `res.rows[0]?.ok` for `try` mode (:132), so the helper reports `{acquired: true}` and runs `fn` completely unserialized — a fail-OPEN on a money path, with no log line and no error. It is not reachable from today's three callers (orders.controller.ts:101 narrows `dto.customerId` to truthy; the service takes `customerId: string`; buyer.controller.ts uses guard-populated `ctx.customerId`), but the module is explicitly built for reuse — discovery.md says PR-3's cron leader lock consumes this same helper — and this codebase reaches for `!` assertions freely on the very same value three lines below the lock call (orders.controller.ts:142, :154). Nothing in T1 or T4 would notice: T1 mocks the pg client entirely, so NULL-argument semantics never execute.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Guard at the top of withAdvisoryLock: reject a non-string or empty `family`/`key` with LockUnavailableError (or a TypeError) before connecting, and state the fail-open reason in the doc comment so future families cannot inherit it.
remainingFindings.decision: node-postgres binds undefined as NULL, hashtext(NULL) is NULL, pg_advisory_lock is strict and takes no lock, and wait mode hard-codes acquired=true, so a nullish key runs fn with no mutual exclusion and no signal. Not reachable from today's three callers, but the helper is explicitly built for reuse (PR-3 cron leader lock); a one-line guard on empty family/key closes a fail-open on a money primitive.

remainingFindings.summary: sweepAllPendingOrders swallows every ConflictException/ServiceUnavailableException by exception type rather than by lock cause, and its return value cannot distinguish a customer skipped for contention from one with nothing to merge.
remainingFindings.detail: orders.service.ts:1486-1498 wraps `mergeAllPendingForCustomer(g.customerId)` in `catch (e) { if (e instanceof ConflictException || e instanceof ServiceUnavailableException) { logger.warn(...); continue; } throw e; }` and returns `{customers: groups.length, merged}`. Two consequences. (a) The filter is by TYPE, not by cause: any ConflictException raised from deep inside the merge body — the transaction at :860+, `recomputeLineCategoryTaxes`, or (for the sibling `forceConsolidateCustomer` shape) `invoicesService.reconcileOrderDraftInvoice` — is now silently absorbed by the hourly cron and the `POST /orders/sweep` endpoint (orders.controller.ts:419) as if it were lock contention. Before this change any such error aborted the sweep loudly. (b) `merged` is only incremented on a truthy winner, and `mergeAllPendingForCustomer` also returns null when there was nothing to merge, so the response `{customers: 2, merged: 1}` (the exact shape pinned by orders.merge-lock.spec.ts T3-d) is identical whether the second customer was skipped because of a 20 s lock timeout or because they had a single pending order. An operator who presses "Consolidate all" during contention is told it succeeded, with the only evidence in a server log line.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Narrow the catch to the lock cause (check the ConflictException body's `code === "MERGE_IN_PROGRESS"`, or catch LockTimeoutError/LockUnavailableError inside mergeAllPendingForCustomer's caller before they are mapped), and return a `skipped` count alongside `customers`/`merged` so the endpoint's caller can see contention.
remainingFindings.decision: The sweep's catch at :1486-1498 filters by exception type, so any ConflictException/ServiceUnavailableException from inside the merge body is now absorbed by the hourly cron and POST /orders/sweep as if it were contention, where before it aborted loudly; and the {customers, merged} return cannot show a skipped customer. Discriminating on the MERGE_IN_PROGRESS code (or catching the lock errors before they are mapped) fixes both.

remainingFindings.summary: Waiters pin a pool connection for the whole 20 s wait, so contention on ONE customer exhausts the 8-slot pool and denies merges to every OTHER customer with a 503.
remainingFindings.detail: db-locks.ts:60-73 builds the lock pool with `max: 8` and `connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000`, and every caller — holder AND waiter — occupies one slot for the full critical section or the full `waitMs: 20_000` wait, because the wait happens inside `client.query(pg_advisory_lock ...)` on an already-checked-out client (:132). Concrete scenario: one busy customer receives 8 near-simultaneous merges (two scanners plus a buyer submit plus the cron sweep plus retries). One runs; seven sit blocked in Postgres holding all remaining slots. A ninth request — a merge for a COMPLETELY UNRELATED customer, which has no contention at all — cannot check out a connection, waits 5 s, and gets LockUnavailableError -> 503 "Merge lock unavailable". Head-of-line blocking on one key therefore takes out the whole merge subsystem for that API process, and (per the finding on orders.controller.ts:221) that 503 can land on a request whose order row has already committed. The pool sizing note in the spec's Deploy day section reasons only about the total connection budget, not about waiters occupying slots.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Decouple waiting from the pool: shorten waitMs (see the mobile-timeout finding), or acquire with `mode: "try"` plus a bounded application-level retry so a blocked caller releases its connection between attempts, or size the pool for expected concurrent waiters rather than expected concurrent holders.
remainingFindings.decision: Holders and waiters both pin a slot for the full critical section or the full 20 s wait, so eight merges on one hot customer exhaust the pool and an unrelated customer's uncontended merge hits the 5 s checkout timeout and gets 503. Real head-of-line blocking per API process; partly a designed capacity limit, but with #5 it compounds into 503s on paths that (per #1) can land after commit.

remainingFindings.summary: A fourth post-commit merge caller exists outside the controller/buyer/sweep set the fix rounds looked at: createOrderFromTemplate commits the order at :395 and then calls mergeAllPendingForCustomer at :418 with no catch, so the new 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS / 503 escapes to the client after the order row already exists — and the manual endpoint that reaches it has no idempotency guard, so the retry the error message invites duplicates the standing order.
remainingFindings.detail:
Call-site read (the question the decider asked me to settle: is there a fourth path?). Callers of the two now-locked service methods are: orders.controller.ts:203 (staff post-merge sweep), orders.controller.ts:221 (non-staff create sweep), buyer.controller.ts:661 and :688 (buyer sweeps), orders.service.ts:1487 (sweepAllPendingOrders — this one DID get a per-customer catch, verified at orders.service.ts:1488-1497), orders.controller.ts:426 (forceConsolidate endpoint — a bare pass-through with nothing committed before it, so it is fine), and order-templates.service.ts:418. That last one is in no work package, no spec covers it (order-templates.service.spec.ts:48 stubs mergeAllPendingForCustomer to resolve null), and it is the shape the fix rounds were worried about.

Failure path, concrete: an OPERATOR or CUSTOMER hits POST /order-templates/:id/generate (order-templates.controller.ts:88-93, @Roles(OPERATOR, CUSTOMER)) -> generateOrderForUser -> generateOrder (:217) -> createOrderFromTemplate. Line 395 commits `prisma.forTenant().order.create({...lineItems: {create: lineItemsData}})` — a standalone write, no enclosing transaction. Line 418 then calls `this.ordersService.mergeAllPendingForCustomer(template.customerId)`, which now (orders.service.ts:818, :1150-1158) can throw ConflictException{code:'MERGE_IN_PROGRESS'} on a 20s lock_timeout or ServiceUnavailableException when the 8-connection lock pool cannot hand out a client within connectionTimeoutMillis 5_000 (db-locks.ts:69-73). Nothing between :418 and the HTTP layer catches either. So: order committed, request answered 409/503.

Why that is money, not cosmetics: the manual path has NO idempotency guard — only the cron has one (`existing` check at :286-295). generateOrder mints a fresh `orderNumber = ORD-${Date.now()}` every call. The 409 body's message is literally "Another merge for this customer is in progress — retry.", and in the web dashboard it reaches the user as a toast (app/providers.tsx:36-38 — MERGE_IN_PROGRESS is not in HANDLED_CODES). The user retries -> a SECOND identical template order is created -> the next successful merge (hourly @Cron at orders.service.ts:1520) folds both into one winner, and mergeBoxedContributions SUMS the winner line with the loser contributions, so the customer's standing order lands at 2x quantity and invoices at 2x.

The cron path (generateDailyOrders :297-307) does catch, but miscounts: the order was created, yet the catch logs "Failed to generate order for template ..." and the template counts in neither totalCreated nor totalSkipped.

NOTE FOR DEDUPE: orders.controller.ts:221 (`create()` commits, then mergeAllPendingForCustomer with no catch) is the same shape; if the standing #0/#1 candidates only cover :203 and the buyer sweeps, :221 needs the same treatment. buyer.controller.ts:615-621 already states this exact rule in prose ("a throw here would report a merge that DID land as a failure ... the same cart would be added a second time") and applies best-effort catching to applyBuyerMergeHeader — then calls the sweep three lines later at :661 with no catch.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Make every post-commit sweep best-effort: wrap order-templates.service.ts:418 (and orders.controller.ts:221 / :203, buyer.controller.ts:661 if not already in the #0/#1 fix) in try/catch that logs the lock error and continues with the already-created/merged order, exactly as buyer.controller.ts:622-638 does for applyBuyerMergeHeader. A merge sweep that could not take the lock is deferred work the hourly cron will finish, not a failed request.
remainingFindings.decision: The call-site read establishes a fourth post-commit caller the fix rounds never touched: createOrderFromTemplate commits the order row, then calls the now-locked mergeAllPendingForCustomer with no catch, so the change's new 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS / 503 escapes to the client after the order exists and the generate endpoint has no idempotency guard, so the retry the message invites creates a duplicate standing order. Its spec stubs the merge to resolve null, so nothing pins this; the same per-customer catch applied to sweepAllPendingOrders belongs here.

remainingFindings.summary: Severity evidence for the post-commit-throw candidate: the web staff-merge posts DELTA items with no Idempotency-Key, so the server's in-lock replay guard can never fire for the dashboard — a 409 MERGE_IN_PROGRESS raised after the fold committed is indistinguishable from one raised before it, and the retry the toast asks for folds the same delta a second time.
remainingFindings.detail:
This settles the decider's second question. Payload shape: submitOrder builds `itemsForSubmit` at :902-927 purely from the modal's own `lineItems` (the new cart), NOT from the existing order's lines, and posts them with `mergeChoice: 'merge'` (:943). Server side, orders.controller.ts:158 does `foldMergeItems(current.lineItems ?? [], dto.items ?? [])` and writes the result with `replaceAll: true` (:168) — i.e. the delta is ADDED to whatever is currently stored. Re-posting the same body after a committed fold therefore double-counts (10 + 3 -> 13, retry -> 16), which is precisely the lost-update arithmetic the T2 concurrency pin exercises.

The one server-side guard against that is the replay check inside the lock (orders.controller.ts:151-157, findOrderIdByIdempotencyKey + recordIdempotencyKey at :180-182), and it is keyed on the `Idempotency-Key` header (:89, :93). The web client never sends one: useCreateOrder (apps/web/lib/api/orders.ts:277) is `apiClient.post("/orders", dto)` with no config, and the axios request interceptor (apps/web/lib/api-client.ts:103-121) attaches only Authorization and X-Tenant-Slug. The only idempotency work in the web app is in ScanInvoiceModal (a different flow). Mobile, by contrast, DOES send one per cart session (apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts, apps/mobile/lib/api/orders.ts:206) — so mobile is protected from this and the dashboard is not.

Retry is not hypothetical, it is instructed: MERGE_IN_PROGRESS is absent from HANDLED_CODES in app/providers.tsx:22-35, so MutationCache.onError toasts `data.message` = "Another merge for this customer is in progress — retry." (providers.tsx:37-38). onError in this file (:967-987) handles only MERGE_CHOICE_REQUIRED and the regulated-license block and does not call onClose(), so the modal stays open with the cart intact; the operator clicks Create Order again, gets the merge prompt again (:1034-1038), picks Merge (:1997), and the same delta is folded onto the already-merged order.

When the 409 comes from the lock ACQUIRE (LockTimeoutError, db-locks.ts:139-146) nothing was written and the retry is correct. When it comes from the post-commit sweep (orders.controller.ts:203) the write DID land and the retry over-charges. Both produce byte-identical 409 bodies. So the fix cannot live only in a client-side idempotency key — the controller must stop turning a post-commit sweep failure into an error response — but the missing Idempotency-Key is what removes the last safety net for the dashboard and should be closed alongside it.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Fix the server side first (make the post-merge sweep best-effort so a merge that committed is never reported as a failure). Additionally, mint one Idempotency-Key per CreateOrderModal cart session (mirroring apps/mobile/lib/order-submit-key.ts) and pass it as the Idempotency-Key header from useCreateOrder, so any retry of a merge that already landed replays instead of re-folding.
remainingFindings.decision: The payload evidence is solid: the dashboard posts delta items re-folded onto the stored lines with replaceAll and never sends an Idempotency-Key, so any 409 that escapes after the fold committed double-counts on the retry the toast requests. Whether such a post-commit 409 can reach the dashboard hinges on the controller's :203/:221 post-merge sweeps and the buyer's :661/:688 sweeps having been wrapped like sweepAllPendingOrders was — the evidence only verified the service sweep's catch, not those four — so this stays real until a fixer confirms every post-commit sweep in the controllers is caught (and if it is, the candidate collapses to a pre-existing client gap, not a defect of this change).

remainingFindings.summary: A fifth merge writer bypasses the new lock entirely: this backfill script re-implements the customer merge with its own PrismaClient and takes no advisory lock, so the invariant railway.toml, CLAUDE.md and the code map now assert ("order merges are cross-replica safe", "never add a second lock") is false for it.
remainingFindings.detail:
The PR's whole claim is that every customer-level merge serializes on ('order-merge', customerId): apps/api/railway.toml:9-12 now says "Order merges are cross-replica safe: staff create(), buyer createOrder and mergeAllPendingForCustomer/forceConsolidateCustomer serialize on a customer-keyed Postgres advisory lock", and .claude/code-map/api.md:604-611 enumerates the same four entry points. apps/api/scripts/merge-pending-orders.js is a fifth writer of the same rows and it is not in that set: it builds its own `new Pool({connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL})` + PrismaClient (:22-23), groups customers with >1 mergeable PENDING order (:26-38), and under `--execute` (:19, :42-46) re-reads and folds each customer's orders itself — the header even says "Mirrors OrdersService.mergeAllPendingForCustomer" (:4).

Failure scenario: an operator runs `node apps/api/scripts/merge-pending-orders.js --execute` against production (the documented usage at :11-13) while the API's hourly sweep (@Cron("0 * * * *"), orders.service.ts:1520) or a live staff merge is folding the same customer. The script reads the same PENDING orders, the API's locked merge commits, and the script then writes its own absolute totals derived from the pre-merge snapshot — the exact lost update B199 describes, silently, with no error. The advisory lock cannot help because the script never asks for it. The residual risk is small (a manual, one-shot backfill) but it is exactly the risk the new railway.toml comment tells a future reader no longer exists.
remainingFindings.fixHint: Either have the script take the same lock per customer before its fold (require the compiled db-locks helper, or issue pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('order-merge'), hashtext(customerId)) on its own pg client for each customer), or, if it is truly dead, delete it — and in either case make railway.toml/CLAUDE.md/api.md name the complete set of merge writers so the invariant stays checkable.
remainingFindings.decision: apps/api/scripts/merge-pending-orders.js re-implements the customer fold with its own Pool/PrismaClient under --execute and takes no advisory lock, so the invariant railway.toml, CLAUDE.md and the code map now assert is false for that writer. It is an operator-run backfill, not a request path, so the practical race window is narrow; the cheap fix is to take the same ('order-merge', customerId) lock in the script or document it as an offline-only tool.
